title: Direct Realism & Enactivism
summary: Direct Realism & Enactivism as counterpoints to Representationalism challenge the idea that perception and memory rely on inner representations. They argue that mind is constituted through direct contact with the world and through embodied action within it.
summary_html: Direct Realism & Enactivism as counterpoints to Representationalism challenge the idea that perception and memory rely on inner representations. They argue that mind is constituted through direct contact with the world and through embodied action within it.
content_html:
Direct Realism & Enactivism — One Pager

Direct Realism

  • We perceive objects directly, not via internal intermediaries.
  • Perceptual experience is awareness of external objects as they are.
  • Memory is re-experiencing aspects of those direct encounters, not manipulating stored images.
  • Denies the need for mental “representations” that stand in for the world.

Enactivism

  • Cognition is embodied action: knowing is doing.
  • Perception arises through sensorimotor engagement — not constructing pictures but enacting a world through skillful interaction.
  • Memory: patterns of readiness-to-act, re-enacted in new contexts; a dynamical skill rather than stored content.
  • Highlights feedback loops: mind is continuous with body and environment.

Memory

  • Memory as re-engagement
  • Habits and embodied traces
  • Narrative as enacted meaning
  • Ecological & social grounding

Analysis

  • Avoids the homunculus problem (no inner observer of representations).
  • Explains perception as world-involving, not confined to brain states.
  • Connects memory to embodied skill, habit, and ecological engagement.

but...

  • Hard to explain illusions, hallucinations, and false memories without representational content.
  • May underestimate the brain’s role in constructing predictive internal models.
  • Risk of oversimplification when applied to abstract or symbolic thought.

References

  • Chemero, A. (2009). Radical embodied cognitive science. MIT Press. https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262516476
  • Gibson, J. J. (1979). The ecological approach to visual perception. Houghton Mifflin. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203767764
  • Hutto, D., & Myin, E. (2013). Radicalizing enactivism. MIT Press. https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262018536
  • Noë, A. (2004). Action in perception. MIT Press. https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262640478
